Name: Siya Patil
Question: What is it that you find most attractive about people?
Answer: Kindness. I think kindness is the most important value that attracts me to people. It is the single most underrated virtue. But so, so essential. You can have all the smarts, money, good looks but if you don’t have kindness, what use is any of the above. How you treat others, how you make others feel, that’s what really matters in the end. As I grow older, a lot of things that felt important at some point have started losing their charm. The best looking guy may be a jerk to the waiter, the girl in the BMW might just kick a puppy, the guy with a Harvard degree may be a bully. Of course material things are exciting and fun, but if you are not kind, you cannot form a genuine bond with anyone. How you treat others matters. How you make others feel matters. We need to start adding “people” in our lives and not portfolios. At the end of the day, after all the spotlights dim, people are only going to remember how you made them feel. So ask yourself…. Are you kind to the stranger on the street? Are you kind to your friends and family? Are you kind to yourself?

Name: Siya Patil
Question: What does a mental breakdown feel like?
Answer: It feels horrible. You feel like a deflated balloon. I have been studying for my PG entrance. It's a highly, highly competitive exam with 1.5 lakh doctors competing for like 15k seats. This year, I had a good score. I had a very good chance of getting a seat of my choice. I went to Delhi for my councelling, waiting outside the hall I had a mental breakdown, a full blown panic attack. After waiting all day, 5 minutes from my turn I ran away from the place. I literally ran away to the main Street, took a cab and reached the airport 6 hours before my flight. In my mind I knew what a gigantic mistake I am making and yet I couldn't stop myself. It was after the flight landed at my home town and I realised the magnitude of what happened. I have cried for the past 5 days straight. And it isn't that cute silent tears cry, it's an outright ugly, wailing cry. What wouldn't I give to go back there and somehow control my panic attack. In one moment of panic I lost a thing I have worked my ass off for 3 years. So how does a mental breakdown feel like? It feels f**king horrible. You feel so helpless, like you're captive of your own mind. Every rational cell in your body will tell you you're wrong and yet you cannot stop yourself. Like there a fog stopping you from seeing clearly. And it happens to the best of us. I am a doctor, I work as a general practitioner, seeing 80–130 patients daily. I do all that without any glitch. And yet, when the mental breakdown happened, I couldn't help myself. I crushed my dreams, I wandered around in a strange city without thinking of my safety and now I am left with a dead end and tremendous guilt. Why didn't I seek help earlier? I don't have depression or anxiety or any other mental health condition. That's the thing about mental breakdowns, it's as unexpected as it is unpleasant.

Question: How do doctors handle patient complaints and how does it impact their relationship with the patient?
Answer: I think every doctor faces this sometime or the other. Medicine is a high stakes field. Every single thing we do affects the patients so intimately, even a small mistake can be a cause of a lot anguish and complaints (often rightfully so). I often say to my non-medico husband, when you make mistakes your company might lose some money but when I make mistakes, people die. So, once you understand this concept, a doctor can become more empathetic towards patient’s complaints. Initially, I used to get very worked up with even the smallest of complaints by the patients. I used to rack my brains, thinking how could I go wrong. But as time has passed, I have realised the key to actually solve the problem is to not take it personally. Patients are usually already worried with their illnesses, so their complaints have a lot to do with their general state of distress. So just be, empathetic. Understand where the dissatisfaction is coming from. And if you see any mistakes from your side, just come forth with 100% honesty. In my experience, this approach usually works. Patients appreciate an honest and truthful dialogue. So just accept your mistake, remedy it and don’t repeat it the next time. You’ll gain that patient’s trust for life. As for me, even if the patient complains; it absolutely does not affect my relationship with them. I don’t believe doctors are above mistakes and consequences. We are human, we can make mistakes and when we do, people have the right to complaint. I do, however, have zero tolerance policy towards violence. So if a patient starts getting aggressive with his complaints, I usually refer them to another specialist.

Question: What was the most messed up punishment(s) you received as a child?
Answer: I had forgotten about this, but remembered after reading the answers. It happened to my classmate but I would still like to share just to highlight how sometimes the the education system gets it horribly wrong. I was in 6th grade (about 11–12 years old) I went to a very strict convent, and we had very definite rules about hair and dressing. One such rule was for boys to have extremely short hair, like so short that they shouldn't be able to grab. One of my friends had not cut his hair in a while and had recieved a prior warning. That day during morning inspection, his hair were still not cut. The teacher grabbed his hair, tied a tiny ponytail on the top, rubbed the chalk dust from the duster all over his face then went ahead to parade him in EVERY SINGLE classroom. All 40 of them (4 divisions each from class 1 to 10). Even as a kid I was horrified at my friend's ordeal. But now, as an adult and as a doctor, I shudder to think the emotional trauma that kid must have gone through. That too for a few extra inches of hair? Schools tend to stress too much on discipline and forget the innocence, the freedom that helps us actually grow. Was the long hair more harmful to his psych or the humiliation?
